blocks.text: Public Administration is the **action part of government** — 'the detailed and systematic execution of public law' (**Woodrow Wilson**, whose 1887 essay *The Study of Administration* founded the discipline). **L.D. White**: it consists of 'all those operations having for their purpose the fulfilment or enforcement of public policy'. **Herbert Simon** narrowed the lens to **decision-making** ('administration is the art of getting things done'), while **Dwight Waldo** insisted it is ultimately a field of **political theory** — administration is never value-neutral.

rows: **P**lanning, **O**rganising, **S**taffing, **D**irecting, **CO**-ordinating, **R**eporting, **B**udgeting — the managerial techniques view; criticised as ignoring substantive policy and values
What agencies actually do — law & order, welfare, health, education, defence: services cannot be reduced to techniques
Broad (White): all three organs' administrative work; Narrow (Simon, Luther Gulick): only the executive branch
Integral (Henri Fayol/White): all workers, manual to managerial; Managerial (Simon/Gulick): only those who plan, organise, command

blocks.text: **Public vs private administration**: they share management techniques (**Fayol**: one administrative science), but differ in the **public interest test, legal framework, accountability to legislature and citizen, equality of treatment, monopoly and coercive power, and fishbowl transparency** (**Paul Appleby**: government is 'different because it is public'; **Sir Josiah Stamp**'s four differentiators).

sections.heading: Nature and evolution — paradigms in one sweep

items: **Politics–administration dichotomy (1887–1926)** — Wilson, **Goodnow** (*Politics and Administration*): politics decides, administration executes.
**Principles era (1927–37)** — Willoughby, Gulick: universal 'principles'; the discipline's high noon.
**Era of challenge (1938–47)** — Simon's *Administrative Behavior* (principles are mere 'proverbs'); the human-relations turn (**Hawthorne studies, Elton Mayo**).
**Crisis of identity (1948–70)** — behaviouralism; comparative PA (**F.W. Riggs** — prismatic-sala model for developing societies).
**New Public Administration (Minnowbrook I, 1968)** — relevance, **values, social equity**, change; 'a client-oriented administration'.
**New Public Management (1980s–90s)** — Hood's term: markets, managerialism, 'steering not rowing' (**Osborne & Gaebler**); agencification, performance pay.

**Post-NPM / New Public Service & governance (2000s–)** — **Denhardt & Denhardt**: 'serve citizens, not customers'; networks, digital-era governance, collaborative and participatory administration — the SDG-era frame.

flowchart TD

  B --> C[Simon's challenge - decisions and behaviour]
  C --> D[Comparative and development administration - Riggs]
  D --> E[New Public Administration 1968 - equity and values]
  E --> F[New Public Management 1990s - markets and managers]
  F --> G[New Public Service and governance - citizens and networks]

sections.heading: Why it matters in India — and in AP

items: The Indian state is a **development administration** (Edward Weidner: administration geared to progressive political, economic and social objectives): planning, welfare delivery, and now **mission-mode digital governance**.

Scope keeps widening: from law-and-order night-watchman to **regulator, enabler, facilitator** — LPG reforms shifted the state's role, but welfare scale (NFSA, MGNREGA, DBT) keeps administration central.

**AP as a living lab**: the **village/ward secretariat system** (one secretariat per ~2,000 population), functionary-at-doorstep volunteers, and DBT-heavy welfare architecture are a textbook case of Weberian field bureaucracy meeting NPM-style citizen-charter delivery — use it as your illustration for 'scope of public administration today'.

blocks.text: Exam tip: Definitions (Wilson, White, Simon) + POSDCORB + public/private distinction + seven-stage evolution is the complete skeleton. One AP illustration converts a theory answer into an APPSC answer.

prelimsPointers: **Woodrow Wilson** — 'father of Public Administration'; essay: *The Study of Administration* (**1887**).
**POSDCORB** coined by **Luther Gulick** (Papers on the Science of Administration, 1937).
**Herbert Simon** won the **Nobel Prize (Economics, 1978)** for bounded rationality / decision-making.
**Minnowbrook Conference I (1968)** under **Dwight Waldo** launched New Public Administration; Minnowbrook II (1988), III (2008).
**F.W. Riggs**: prismatic society, 'sala' model — comparative public administration.
*Reinventing Government* (1992) — **Osborne & Gaebler**; NPM slogan 'steering rather than rowing'.
**Paul Appleby** (reports on Indian administration, 1953 & 1956) recommended the **IIPA** and O&M division.
mainsAngles: 'Public administration is public because it is different' — distinguish public from private administration with thinkers.
Trace the evolution of Public Administration from the politics–administration dichotomy to New Public Service.
Is POSDCORB an adequate statement of the scope of public administration? Critically examine.
Development administration remains the defining character of the Indian state — discuss with Andhra Pradesh's delivery architecture as illustration.

glossary.definition: Founding claim (Wilson, Goodnow) that policy-making (politics) and policy-execution (administration) are separable spheres; later demolished as administrators visibly make policy.
Gulick's acronym for the chief executive's functions — Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting, Budgeting.
Simon's insight that decision-makers 'satisfice' rather than maximise, choosing acceptable options under limits of information, time and cognition.
1980s–90s reform wave importing market mechanisms and private-sector management into government — competition, contracting-out, performance measurement.
Administration oriented to planned socio-economic transformation in post-colonial states (Weidner, Riggs) — India's dominant administrative idiom.
Denhardt & Denhardt's post-NPM corrective: the administrator's first job is to serve citizens and build public value, not steer customers.

sections.heading: The Arthashastra — the state as a science

blocks.text: **Kautilya (Chanakya/Vishnugupta)**, minister to **Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321 BCE)**, wrote the **Arthashastra** — 15 books on statecraft, economics and administration, rediscovered by **R. Shamasastry in 1909**. Its premise is startlingly modern: governance is a **science (danda-niti)**, the king is an **employee of the state**, and administration exists for welfare — '**In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness; in their welfare his welfare**' (praja sukhe sukham rajnah).

headers: Element (Saptanga — seven limbs of the state)
rows: Population & geography — the tax and welfare base
Public finance — 'all undertakings depend upon finance'
Foreign relations (the mandala theory of concentric friends/enemies)

items: **Recruitment by merit and test**: amatyas chosen after **upadha (integrity) tests** — dharma, artha, kama and bhaya (fear) tests — the ancient ancestor of integrity screening.

**Departmentalisation**: ~30 **adhyakshas (superintendents)** — of gold, mines, agriculture (sitadhyaksha), trade (panyadhyaksha), shipping, tolls, weights & measures — a proto-ministerial system with detailed job descriptions.

**District & local tiers**: janapada divided into **sthaniya (800 villages), dronamukha (400), kharvatika (200), sangrahana (10)**; the **gopa** and **sthanika** as field officers — the lineage of India's district administration.

**Public finance**: land revenue (bhaga, typically 1/6), tolls, fines; budgeting, audit by **samaharta (collector-general)** and **sannidhata (treasurer)**; strictures against embezzlement — Kautilya lists **40 ways officials swallow revenue** ('just as fish moving in water cannot be known when drinking it').
**Intelligence & vigilance**: an elaborate espionage network (gudhapurusha) — stationary and wandering spies — for corruption control and state security.
**Justice & welfare**: dharmasthiya (civil) and kantakashodhana (criminal/administrative) courts; famine relief, support for widows/orphans/aged, consumer protection (price/weights regulation).

items: **Modern echoes**: merit recruitment (UPSC/APPSC), integrity testing and vigilance (CVC), the district collector (samaharta's descendant), performance budgeting, welfare state (praja-sukha), consumer protection, disaster relief — even the **Yogakshema** phrase in LIC's motto is Kautilyan.

**Critiques**: amoral realpolitik (ends-justify-means in foreign policy), pervasive surveillance, monarchic frame — but as **ARC and administrative historians note**, the Arthashastra's core is **accountable, audited, welfare-oriented bureaucracy**, not despotism.

**AP hook**: Mauryan administration reached the Andhra region (Ashokan inscriptions; the Satavahanas, who ruled from Amaravati/Dharanikota, inherited and adapted Mauryan administrative forms) — link ancient administrative continuity to the state's own heritage.

blocks.text: Exam tip: Quote 'praja sukhe sukham rajnah' + the fish-in-water line on corruption. Structure: saptanga → machinery (recruitment, departments, revenue, spies) → relevance table to modern institutions. Examiners reward explicit ancient-to-modern mapping.

prelimsPointers: Arthashastra: **15 adhikaranas (books)**; rediscovered and published by **R. Shamasastry (1909)**.
**Saptanga** theory: swami, amatya, janapada, durga, kosha, danda, mitra.
**Samaharta** = collector-general of revenue; **Sannidhata** = chief treasurer.
Land revenue was typically **one-sixth (shadbhaga)** of produce.
**Upadha tests** screened ministers for integrity through dharma, artha, kama and bhaya temptations.
Kautilya enumerated **40 modes of embezzlement** and prescribed graded punishments and informer rewards.
**Mandala theory**: the circle-of-states doctrine of foreign policy; four upayas — **sama, dana, bheda, danda**.
mainsAngles: 'The Arthashastra is a manual of the welfare state written two millennia early' — examine with reference to its administrative ideas.
Map Kautilya's saptanga and revenue administration onto the institutions of modern Indian governance.
Kautilya's anti-corruption framework combined deterrence, surveillance and incentives — evaluate its contemporary relevance for vigilance administration.
Compare the Kautilyan district chain (sthaniya–gopa) with the modern district collector system.

glossary.definition: Kautilya's theory of the state as seven interdependent limbs — sovereign, ministers, territory-people, fort, treasury, force and ally.
The science of governance/coercion — Kautilya's term for statecraft, resting on the just use of sanction (danda) to uphold order.
Kautilyan compound for acquisition (yoga) and secure enjoyment (kshema) of welfare — the state's welfare duty; echoed in modern Indian public institutions.
Departmental superintendent in Mauryan administration (e.g., of mines, trade, agriculture) — the ancient counterpart of a head of department.
Kautilya's secret agents — stationary (samstha) and roving (sanchara) spies used for vigilance, intelligence and public-opinion sensing.

sections.heading: Mughal administration — the centralised imperial machine

blocks.text: The Mughal system (perfected under **Akbar**) was a **centralised, military-bureaucratic** empire run through the **mansabdari system**: every officer held a **mansab (rank)** with dual **zat** (personal status/salary) and **sawar** (cavalry obligation) grades — a unified civil-military service where office, not birth, fixed rank, though loyalty ran to the emperor personally. Salaries were often paid through **jagirs** (revenue assignments — transferable, non-hereditary), keeping officials dependent on the crown.

rows: Revenue & finance head — the empire's CFO
Military pay & mansab administration — head of the military-personnel department
**Subedar** (governor), **Diwan** (provincial revenue — deliberately independent of the subedar: an early check-and-balance), Bakshi, Sadr, Kotwal (town police), Faujdar (district law & order)

items: **Land revenue**: **Todar Mal's zabti/dahsala system** — measurement (paimaish), classification (polaj, parauti, chachar, banjar) and cash rates from ten-year averages — the ancestor of ryotwari-style settlement science.

Weaknesses: personalised loyalty, **jagirdari crisis** (assignments outran revenue by Aurangzeb's time), no rule of law above the emperor, negligible citizen-state relation — administration extracted more than it served.

sections.heading: British rule — the colonial grammar of Indian administration

items: **Civil service**: **Cornwallis** professionalised the covenanted service (the 'steel frame' — Lloyd George's phrase); **Macaulay Committee (1854)** brought **open competitive merit recruitment**; Indians entered slowly (Satyendranath Tagore, 1863; simultaneous exams only in 1922).
**District administration**: the **Collector (created 1772, Warren Hastings)** fused revenue, magisterial and executive power — still the pivot of Indian and AP field administration.
**Rule of law & codification**: Macaulay's **IPC (1860)**, CrPC, Evidence Act (1872), civil codes — replaced by BNS/BNSS/BSA only in **2023–24**, showing the longevity of the colonial legal frame.
**Police**: **Police Act, 1861** — a regime-security force answerable upward, not to citizens; its design endures (hence repeated reform demands: NPC 1977–81, **Prakash Singh, 2006**).

**Revenue settlements**: **Permanent Settlement (1793, Bengal — zamindari)**, **Ryotwari (Munro & Read — Madras Presidency, covering coastal Andhra & Rayalaseema)**, **Mahalwari** (North-West) — each with lasting agrarian consequences.

**Other legacies**: budgeting & audit (the CAG's ancestry), railways/telegraph/PWD, census & gazetteers, secretariat system, local self-government (**Ripon's 1882 resolution**), and a tradition of **district gazetteer-based knowledge governance**.

sections.heading: Assessment — continuity, change and the AP lens

items: **What independent India kept**: the generalist civil service, district collector, secretariat, police structure, tehsil/revenue machinery, audit — 'continuity with change': the same steel frame re-purposed from **extraction to development** (Appleby's caution: structures built for control adapt poorly to welfare).

**What it changed**: constitutional supremacy over executive discretion, universal franchise, fundamental rights, Panchayati Raj, and (slowly) citizen-centric instruments — RTI, charters, e-governance.

**AP lens**: **Sir Thomas Munro's ryotwari** in the Madras Presidency shaped coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema's direct cultivator-state relation (contrast with zamindari estates abolished by the **Madras Estates Abolition Act, 1948**); the district collector remains AP's delivery pivot, now flanked by secretariats and volunteers — the newest layer on a Mauryan-Mughal-British palimpsest.

blocks.text: Exam tip: The examiner wants lineage, not just description: mansabdari → merit service → IAS; Todar Mal → Munro's ryotwari → AP revenue administration; Police Act 1861 → Prakash Singh. Two continuity chains and one critique (extraction vs welfare design) make a complete answer.

prelimsPointers: **Mansabdari**: dual ranks — **zat** (personal) and **sawar** (cavalry); introduced under **Akbar**.
**Todar Mal** (Akbar's diwan) devised the **dahsala/zabti** revenue system.
Office of **Collector**: created **1772** under **Warren Hastings**.
**Macaulay Committee (1854)** — open competition for the civil service; first ICS exam 1855 (London).
**Ryotwari** system: **Thomas Munro** & Alexander Read, Madras Presidency — direct settlement with the ryot (cultivator).
**Police Act, 1861** followed the 1860 Police Commission after the 1857 revolt.
**Ripon's Resolution on local self-government: 1882** — 'Magna Carta of local self-government'.
IPC 1860 / CrPC / Evidence Act 1872 replaced by **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, Sakshya Adhiniyam (in force 1 July 2024)**.
mainsAngles: Mughal administration was a revenue-military machine with sophisticated checks — examine with reference to mansabdari and the provincial diwan.
'Independent India inherited a structure of control and asked it to deliver welfare' — critically assess the British administrative legacy.
Trace the evolution of the district collector from Warren Hastings to the present, with Andhra Pradesh illustrations.
Compare zamindari and ryotwari settlements and their long-run agrarian legacies in coastal Andhra.

glossary.definition: Mughal system of ranked imperial service (mansab = rank) combining civil and military hierarchy, with zat and sawar grades fixing pay and cavalry obligations.
Transferable, non-hereditary assignment of land revenue to a mansabdar in lieu of salary; its scarcity produced the late-Mughal 'jagirdari crisis'.
Todar Mal's cash revenue settlement based on measured area, crop classification and ten-year average yields and prices.
Epithet for the ICS — the small, elite, merit-recruited service that held colonial (and then independent) India's administration together.
Munro-Read revenue system settling land revenue directly with the cultivating ryot, dominant in the Madras Presidency including coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema.
Company-era senior service bound by covenant, ancestor of the ICS/IAS; distinguished from the uncovenanted subordinate services.
